lesson.title: Signal and noise

steps.headline: Four things that can happen on a night

lead.text: Take one guard on one night. Either a thief comes or none does, and either the guard shouts or stays quiet. That gives four outcomes. If a thief comes and the guard shouts, it is a hit. If a thief comes and the guard stays quiet, it is a miss. If no thief comes and the guard shouts anyway, it is a false alarm. If no thief comes and the guard stays quiet, it is a correct rejection.

Two of those outcomes are mistakes, and they are different mistakes. To measure each one we divide by the nights where it could happen. The hit rate is the number of hits divided by the number of nights a thief came. The false-alarm rate is the number of false alarms divided by the number of nights no thief came.

Guard A's records show how this works. A thief came on 10 nights and A shouted on every one, which is 10 hits out of 10 and a hit rate of 100%. Of the 10 quiet nights, A shouted on 9, so the false-alarm rate is 90%.
A guard is on watch on a night when a thief does come. Match what happens to one of the four outcomes.

steps.headline: Why even a careful guard gets it wrong

lead.text: A quiet night is never completely quiet. A shadow moves, a gate rattles in the wind, a car door slams down the road. Call everything that is not a thief noise, and call the thief the signal. A night's overall impression is stronger when a thief is there, but the noise varies from night to night, so the impressions are not fixed.

Plot how often each strength of impression occurs and you get two bell-shaped curves, one for quiet nights and one for thief nights. They overlap, because some quiet nights feel more suspicious than some thief nights. The guard has to choose a line along the scale: an impression stronger than this means shout. That line is the criterion.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, the part of the thief curve to the right of the line is the share of thief nights on which the guard shouts, which is the hit rate. The part of the quiet curve to the right of the line is the false-alarm rate. Because the curves overlap, no position of the line gives all the hits and none of the false alarms.

lead.text: The guard can move the criterion without getting any better at the job. Set the line low and the guard shouts at the faintest hint. Nearly every thief night is caught, and many quiet nights are shouted at too. Set the line high and the guard shouts only at strong impressions. False alarms become rare, and some thieves slip past unchallenged.

Moving the line changes both rates in the same direction, so every gain in hits is paid for with more false alarms. Look at the two pictures. The distance between the two curves is the same in both, since moving the line does not change how far apart the curves sit.

afterFigure.text: That distance is set by how much stronger a thief's presence makes the impression and by how well the guard senses it. It is the measure of skill, and the line is not. The next screens turn it into a number.

lead.text: Over twenty nights a thief came on ten of them. Think about the line each guard has set and about how often each one shouts on each kind of night.

The distance between the curves is called d′ (say d-prime), or sensitivity. We cannot see the curves, only the rates, so we turn each rate into a z-score. A z-score says how many standard deviations a position sits above the middle of its curve. The table is standard: a rate of 0.50 gives z = 0, 0.80 gives 0.84, 0.90 gives 1.28 and 0.954 gives 1.68. A rate below one half gives the same size with a minus sign, so 0.20 gives −0.84, 0.10 gives −1.28 and 0.07 gives −1.48.

Then d′ = z(H) − z(FA), where H is the hit rate and FA the false-alarm rate. Guard B shouted on 8 of 10 thief nights, so H = 0.80 and z(H) = 0.84. B shouted on 1 of 10 quiet nights, so FA = 0.10 and z(FA) = −1.28. Subtracting a negative adds its size, so d′ = 0.84 − (−1.28) = 2.12.
A large d′ belongs to a guard who catches most thieves and rarely raises a false alarm. If the shouting ignores what is actually happening, d′ is near zero, even when many thieves get caught.

steps.headline: Find d′ when the hit rate has z = 1.28 and the false-alarm rate has z = −1.28.

lead.text: Another guard has a hit rate of 0.80 and a false-alarm rate of 0.20. The table on the last screen gives their z-scores.

Skill is half the story. The other half is where the guard puts the line, and that is measured by the criterion, written c. It is found from the same two z-scores: c = −[z(H) + z(FA)] ÷ 2. If c is 0 the line sits midway between the two curves. A negative c means the line sits low and the guard says yes readily. A positive c means the line sits high and the guard is cautious.
For Guard B, z(H) = 0.84 and z(FA) = −1.28, so the sum is −0.44. Halving it gives −0.22, and the minus sign in front turns that into c = +0.22. Guard B leans very slightly towards caution.

The two measures answer different questions. Training and practice raise d′. Costs and rewards move c: a guard who is blamed for every missed thief will lower the line, and one who is blamed for waking the street will raise it.
A guard starts shouting more readily because missing a thief has become costly.
A baggage screener flags a bag at the faintest hint of danger. Missing a weapon would be far worse than a delay.

lesson.orientation: Separate how well an observer can tell signal from noise (d′) from how willing they are to say yes.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two guards watch the same car park overnight. Whenever one of them thinks a thief is about, that guard shouts. Over twenty nights a thief really came on ten of them. Guard A shouted on all ten of those nights, and also on nine of the ten quiet nights. Guard B shouted on eight of the ten thief nights and on one quiet night.
Each guard looks good in one way. Guard A never lets a thief through, and Guard B rarely wakes the street for nothing. A single score for how good a guard is would hide that difference.

The same puzzle turns up wherever someone must decide whether something faint is really there, such as a radiologist reading a scan or a screener checking a bag. This lesson takes the guards' records and pulls apart two things that are easy to run together: how well someone can tell a real event from the background, and how ready they are to say yes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll separate how well someone detects a faint event from how readily they say yes, and put a number on each.

recap.keyIdea: A hit rate mixes skill with willingness. d′ measures how well signal is told from noise, and the criterion c measures how readily the observer says yes.

blocks.text: Back at the car park, Guard A's shouting on almost every night showed a line set very low, and Guard B was the better judge of which nights had a thief. You found d′ = 1.68 from z-scores of 0.84 and −0.84, and that a screener with z(H) = 1.68 and z(FA) = 0 has c = −0.84, a lean towards yes.

recap.nextHook: Whether anything faint is noticed at all depends on where attention is pointed, and the next lesson starts with eight cards to sort, four sums and four word puzzles.

questions.prompt: A lifeguard spots swimmers in difficulty with hit rate 0.69 (z = 0.50) and raises false alarms at rate 0.07 (z = −1.48). What is d′?
hints: Subtract z(FA) from z(H).
The false-alarm z-score is negative.
Add 0.50 and 1.48.
questions.onCorrect: Subtract z(FA) from z(H). The false-alarm z-score is negative, so d′ is the sum of their sizes.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the sizes. The false-alarm z-score is negative, so subtracting it adds.
That is only the false-alarm z-score's size. d′ also uses the hit z-score.

questions.prompt: Lowering the criterion so an observer says yes more often increases hits. Which other outcome, on trials with no signal, does it also increase?
hints: Think about the yes responses on trials with no signal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It also increases false alarms: more yes responses when no signal is present.

questions.onCorrect: A lower criterion means more yes answers everywhere, including false alarms on noise trials.

misconceptions.feedback: Lowering the criterion reduces misses. Think about trials with no signal at all.
More yes answers means fewer correct rejections, not more.

questions.prompt: Another guard shouts readily at the same car park. Her hit rate is 0.954 (z = 1.68) and her false-alarm rate is 0.50 (z = 0). What is her d′?
hints: Use the same formula as before with the new z-scores.
The z-score of a 0.50 rate is zero.
Subtract the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d′ = 1.68 − 0 = 1.68. Sensitivity is unchanged; only the criterion moved.

questions.onCorrect: Moving the criterion changed both rates but not the curves, so d′ stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the larger z-score from itself. Use z(H) − z(FA) with these values.
That halves the difference. d′ is the difference itself.

questions.prompt: A thief came on 10 of 20 nights. Guard A shouted on all 10 thief nights and on 9 of the 10 quiet nights. Guard B shouted on 8 of the thief nights and on 1 of the quiet nights. Which guard is better at telling a thief night from a quiet night?
hints: Look at what each guard does on the quiet nights as well.
Does shouting on every night show that a guard can tell the nights apart?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Guard B: he shouts far more often on thief nights than on quiet nights. Guard A shouts almost whatever happens.

questions.onCorrect: Telling nights apart means shouting far more on thief nights than on quiet ones. Guard B's two rates are far apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Guard A shouts on almost every night, thief or not. That shows willingness, not skill.
They shout at different rates on the two kinds of night. Compare each guard's two rates.

questions.prompt: A guard stays quiet on a night when a thief does come. What is that outcome called?
hints: Was a thief there, and did the guard shout or stay quiet?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A thief came and the guard stayed quiet: a miss.

questions.onCorrect: A thief was there and the guard stayed quiet, which is a miss.

misconceptions.feedback: A false alarm is a shout on a night when no thief comes.
A hit is a shout on a night when a thief does come.
A correct rejection is staying quiet on a night when no thief comes.

questions.prompt: What is the hit rate as a percentage?
hints: A hit is a yes on a trial where the signal is present.
Divide by the number of scans with a tumour, not all scans.
Convert 40/50 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The hit rate is hits divided by signal trials, so only scans with a tumour count in the denominator.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of hits. Turn it into a share of the scans that had a tumour.
That is the share of tumour scans she missed. The hit rate is the share she caught.
That is the rate as a decimal. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: An observer has z(H) = 1.5 and z(FA) = −0.5. What is d′?
hints: d′ subtracts the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.
Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Calculate 1.5 + 0.5.
questions.onCorrect: d′ is the distance between the curves: the hit z-score minus the false-alarm z-score.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the sizes. The false-alarm z-score is negative, so subtracting it adds.
That halves the sum of the z-scores. d′ is their difference.

questions.prompt: Why does subtracting z(FA) make d′ larger here?
hints: What is subtracting a negative number the same as?

acceptedIdeas: The false-alarm z-score is below zero, so subtracting it adds its size.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Subtracting a negative number adds its size.

choices.label: The false-alarm z-score is below zero, so subtracting it adds its size.
The minus sign in the formula flips every number it meets.
d′ must always come out larger than either z-score.

questions.onCorrect: Subtracting a negative adds its size, so low false alarms raise d′.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the number after the minus sign changes. The first z-score stays as it is.
d′ is a difference, so it can be smaller than a z-score.

questions.prompt: A guard has a hit rate of 0.80 (z = 0.84) and a false-alarm rate of 0.20 (z = −0.84). What is d′?
hints: d′ subtracts the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.
Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Calculate 0.84 + 0.84.
questions.onCorrect: d′ = z(H) − z(FA), and subtracting a negative z-score adds its size.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats both z-scores as having the same sign. The false-alarm z-score is negative.
That is only one of the two z-scores. d′ combines both.

questions.prompt: An observer starts saying yes more readily because a miss has become costly. What has changed?
hints: Which of the two measures does cost act on?

acceptedIdeas: The criterion has moved, while sensitivity can stay the same.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Costs and rewards move the criterion. The curves have not moved, so sensitivity is the same.

choices.label: Sensitivity has fallen, because she is less careful.
The criterion has moved, while sensitivity can stay the same.
Both have changed, because they measure the same thing.

questions.onCorrect: Costs and rewards move the criterion line. The curves stay put, so d′ stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Saying yes more readily is not carelessness. The line moved, not the curves.
They are separate measures. One can change while the other stays the same.

questions.prompt: A baggage screener has z(H) = 1.68 and z(FA) = 0. What is her criterion location c = −[z(H) + z(FA)]/2?
hints: Add the two z-scores first.
Halve the sum.
Keep the minus sign in front of the bracket.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: c = −(1.68 + 0)/2 = −0.84. A negative c means a bias towards saying yes.

questions.onCorrect: A negative c means a bias towards yes. Halve the sum of the z-scores and keep the minus sign.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. A screener who leans towards yes has a c below zero.
That leaves out the halving. Divide the sum by two.
